title: Decode the 429
brief: Requests start failing with 429 while dashboards show spare quota. Which kind of limit you hit, how the provider counts tokens and where you enforce limits for many consumers are all open.

blocks.caption: Azure documents several 429 causes; these three need different fixes [[r8]]
head: Cause
How you recognize it
What to do
rows: **Quota exceeded**
`x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens` or `-requests` reaches 0 and your own usage is at the assigned TPM
Reduce consumption, raise the assignment, add capacity, or spill over to another deployment
**System capacity throttling**
429s while you are under quota, usually short-lived, with `retry-after-ms`
Retry with backoff and jitter, add a second deployment or region, consider provisioned capacity
**Temporary rate-limit adjustment on Standard**
`x-ratelimit-limit-tokens` is lower than your assigned TPM
Compare the header with the assignment. A quota increase does not fix it, so back off and add headroom elsewhere

blocks.caption: How each provider counts, as of 2026-10-13
head: Dimension
Azure OpenAI in Foundry
OpenAI
Anthropic
rows: **Limit units**
TPM per subscription, region, model and deployment type. RPM follows TPM: 6 per 1,000 TPM for older chat models, 1 per 1,000 for o3 and o4-mini
RPM, RPD, TPM, TPD and IPM per organization and project, per model, by usage tier
Token bucket with continuous refill: RPM, ITPM and OTPM per model class, plus acceleration limits for sharp ramps
**`max_tokens` accounting**
Prompt plus `max_tokens` plus `best_of` counts up front, so `max_tokens: 4000` reserves 4,000 tokens even for a 200-token answer
Counts the larger of `max_tokens` and a character-based estimate
OTPM counts actual output only, so a high `max_tokens` costs nothing
**Window and signals**
RPM enforced over 1 or 10 second windows. Headers `x-ratelimit-limit-requests`, `x-ratelimit-limit-tokens`, `x-ratelimit-remaining-*`, `x-ratelimit-reset-*`. 429 adds `retry-after-ms`
429 `slow_down` and 503 `server_is_overloaded`, which may carry `Retry-After`
Cache reads do not count toward ITPM for most models. At an 80% hit rate, 2,000,000 ITPM handles 10,000,000 input tokens per minute

blocks.text: Put the limit at the gateway

blocks.caption: Where to enforce a limit
head: Option
Scope
Strength
Weakness
rows: **App-side limiter**
One process or service
Sheds load before the call and costs nothing
No view across replicas or consumers
**APIM `llm-token-limit`**
Per `counter-key`: caller, subscription or product
Token-aware rate and quota in one place for many consumers, with attribution
Per-gateway counters, estimates and brief overshoot, covered below
**Provider or deployment quota**
Per deployment
Protects the model deployment from overload
Shared by every consumer, so one noisy consumer starves the others

blocks.title: Policy order at an AI gateway
blocks.alt: Consumers call an API Management gateway. The gateway applies a per-key token limit, then a semantic cache lookup, then forwards to a backend pool with two deployments. The gateway also emits token metrics to Application Insights.
blocks.src:
flowchart LR
  C[Consumers] --> G[APIM gateway]
  G --> L[Token limit per key]
  L --> S[Semantic cache lookup]
  S --> P[Backend pool]
  P --> A[Deployment A]
  P --> B[Deployment B]
  G --> M[Token metrics]
  M --> I[App Insights]
blocks.caption: Limit first so a cold cache cannot overload the backend. The AI gateway covers token limits, token metrics, semantic caching, load balancing and circuit breaking [[r1]].

blocks.title: Per-consumer token rate, monthly quota and token metrics
blocks.code:
<policies>
  <inbound>
    <base />
    <llm-token-limit
        counter-key="@(context.Subscription.Id)"
        tokens-per-minute="50000"
        token-quota="5000000"
        token-quota-period="Monthly"
        estimate-prompt-tokens="true" />
    <llm-emit-token-metric namespace="llm-usage">
      <dimension name="Subscription ID" />
      <dimension name="API ID" />
    </llm-emit-token-metric>
  </inbound>
  <outbound>
    <base />
  </outbound>
</policies>
blocks.caption: Attributes from the policy reference [[r2]] [[r3]]. A rate overrun returns 429 and a quota overrun returns 403, so clients must handle both differently. `estimate-prompt-tokens` is required: `true` estimates prompt tokens before the call, which can reject an over-limit request before it reaches the backend, and `false` uses actual usage from the response.

blocks.title: Gateway gotchas that cause surprise 429s and bad dashboards

items.symptom: A consumer exceeds its limit for a moment
items.cause: Concurrent requests can briefly exceed the token limit, and counters are per gateway, not aggregated across regions
items.fix: Leave headroom below the provider limit, and set per-region limits instead of one global number

items.cause: When estimating, each image counts up to 1,200 tokens, and streaming requests always estimate
items.fix: Raise limits for vision consumers or meter them separately, and check estimates against real usage

items.symptom: A token metric silently stops appearing
items.cause: More than 5 custom dimensions per policy, 100 unique values per dimension or 1,000 active time series per namespace. Excess data is discarded without an error
items.fix: Keep dimensions low-cardinality, such as subscription, API and model. Never use user id or request id

items.symptom: Streamed answers show wrong token counts
items.cause: Some OpenAI models omit usage when streaming, and an interrupted stream gives inaccurate counts
items.fix: Set `include_usage: true` on streaming requests and treat interrupted streams as approximate

quiz.q: A Standard deployment has an assigned 120,000 TPM. Your own metrics show about 19,000 tokens used in the last minute, yet calls return the response below. Which cause fits best?

code.code:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
x-ratelimit-limit-tokens: 20000
x-ratelimit-remaining-tokens: 0
retry-after-ms: 8000

options: Azure temporarily cut the effective limit on this Standard deployment below the assignment
You exceeded your assigned quota, so the fix is to request a higher TPM assignment for the model
The deployment is provisioned and its PTU pool is exhausted, so spillover should handle it
`max_tokens` is set too low, which makes the service reject requests before they run
quiz.explain: The header says the effective limit is 20,000, while 120,000 is assigned, which is the third documented 429 cause. A higher assignment would not change a temporary reduction. A provisioned deployment would not use the Standard headers this way. A low `max_tokens` does not cause rejections.

quiz.q: A service sends 120 requests per minute to an Azure deployment. Each prompt is 1,500 tokens and each request sets `max_tokens` to 4,000 although answers average 300 tokens. How many tokens per minute does the limiter count?
quiz.hint: Azure counts prompt plus max_tokens up front
quiz.explain: Each request counts 1,500 + 4,000 = 5,500 tokens, so 120 x 5,500 = 660,000. Real usage is only 120 x 1,800 = 216,000. Lowering `max_tokens` toward the real answer length frees most of the limit.

quiz.q: Select every true statement about the APIM `llm-token-limit` policy.
options: A rate overrun returns 429 and a quota overrun returns 403
Counters are per gateway and are not aggregated across regions
Streaming requests always use estimated prompt tokens
Concurrent requests can never push a consumer over its limit
quiz.explain: The first three come from the policy reference. The last is false: concurrent requests can briefly exceed the limit, so leave headroom and do not treat the policy as a hard billing cap.

quiz.q: A team moves a workload from Azure OpenAI to Anthropic and lowers `max_tokens` from 4,000 to 400 to stay under limits. What is the effect on rate limiting?
options: It halves 429s, because OTPM reserves the full `max_tokens` up front for every request
No limit benefit, because OTPM counts actual output, and answers may be cut off
It breaks caching, because `max_tokens` is part of the cache key
It lowers ITPM use, because input and output tokens share a single combined bucket
quiz.explain: On Anthropic, OTPM counts actual output only, so a high `max_tokens` costs nothing, and lowering it only risks truncation. The Azure habit does not transfer. `max_tokens` is not part of a cache key, and ITPM and OTPM are separate limits.

takeaways: Azure has several kinds of 429, three of them quota, capacity throttling and a temporary limit cut. Read the headers first
A 429 can appear below quota. Oversized `max_tokens` and short RPM windows are common causes
Providers count differently. Anthropic OTPM ignores `max_tokens` and cache reads for most models
Enforce per-consumer limits at the gateway, and expect estimates, overshoot and per-gateway counters
Keep metric dimensions low-cardinality or data is dropped without an error
